title: Power Cut: Keep or Throw Out Food
about: Helps you look after the food in your fridge and freezer during a power cut, and decide what to keep, refreeze or throw out once you check it. It shows what each New Zealand source says, side by side where they disagree.

sources.name: MPI, Food safety in natural disasters and emergencies
MPI / New Zealand Food Safety fact sheet, Food safety in the home after flooding (Feb 2023)
NEMA Civil Defence consistent messages, Response: What to do in an emergency
Northland Regional Council, Food safety in a power cut
Auckland Regional Public Health Service, Preventing foodborne illness when the power's out
Queenstown Lakes District Council poster, How to keep food safe in a power cut (advice from Public Health Service - Southern)
FSANZ, Food safety in an emergency

warning: If in doubt, throw it out. Don't taste food to see if it's OK. The sources give different times; this app shows each one.
audience: Anyone at home in New Zealand whose power has gone off
version: MPI fact sheet 'Food safety in the home after flooding' (Feb 2023, document 55615); MPI web page 'Food safety in natural disasters and emergencies' (last reviewed 24.02.25); NEMA consistent messages 'Response' and Get Ready 'No power' (no dates shown); Northland Regional Council 'Food safety - power cuts' (no date); ARPHS news item (no date); QLDC poster (Sep 2023); FSANZ 'Food safety in an emergency' (last updated 2 October 2025); all read 19 Nov 2026 NZ time

steps.title: Power cut: what to do now

lines.text: Keep the fridge and freezer doors shut. Open them as little as you can.

quotes.text: During the power failure, open your fridge or freezer as little as possible to help keep it cooler for longer.
The first advice is to not open the door of the refrigerator or freezer.

lines.text: Tell everyone in the house, including the children. A big notice on the door can help.

quotes.text: Make sure you tell everyone in the house including the children. It might be a good idea to hang a big notice on the door to remind everyone.

lines.text: Eat from the fridge first, then the freezer, then the pantry or your emergency kit.

quotes.text: EAT FROM THE FRIDGE FIRST, THE FREEZER SECOND, AND THE PANTRY LAST.
If the power goes out, eat the food from your fridge first, then your freezer. Then eat the food in the cupboard or your emergency kit.

lines.text: Eat foods that will expire soon first, such as bread, meat, salads and dairy products.

quotes.text: Eat foods that will expire soon first – such as bread, meat, salads, and dairy products – because they spoil more quickly than non-perishable food.

lines.text: Leave frozen food in the freezer if you can.

quotes.text: So, leave already frozen food in the freezer if possible.

options.label: Still off: it has just gone off
Still off: it has been off for a while

steps.title: Note when the power went off

lines.text: Tap the button to keep the time in the Log. The app will tell you when each source's fridge or freezer time has passed. Keep this app open (you can go on to the next screens). No source says how to tell how long the power was off if you missed the start.
Power went off

Reminder labels are kept short so four of them fit above the step on a phone; each source's full wording is on the During screen. Reminders start when this screen opens, so they only match the power cut if it really has just started. They run until "The power is back on". The MPI full/half-full day ranges are not reminded (ranges, not one time); they are in the table on the next screen.

quotes.text: An unopened refrigerator will keep your food cool for at least 2 hours.
Unopened fridges should hold refrigeration temperature for 4 hours.
A fridge should keep food cold for around four hours - after that it can begin to spoil.
A freezer shouldn't defrost for around 24 hours.
A freezer that is half full will be okay for up to 24 hours
a full freezer for 48 hours.

MPI, NEMA and the QLDC poster: 4 hours.

quotes.text: Unopened fridges should hold refrigeration temperature for 4 hours.

quotes.text: A fridge should keep food cold for around four hours - after that it can begin to spoil.

lines.text: Northland Regional Council: at least 2 hours.

quotes.text: An unopened refrigerator will keep your food cool for at least 2 hours.

lines.text: How long a freezer stays frozen depends on how full it is, and the sources disagree:

quotes.text: Freezers will remain colder for longer if they are full (2−4 days) compared to if they are half full (1−2 days).
A freezer that is half full will be okay for up to 24 hours and a full freezer for 48 hours.
A freezer shouldn't defrost for around 24 hours.

lines.text: Freezer hold time
No source says what counts as "full" or "half full", or covers a nearly empty freezer.
Every time you open the door, food goes off more quickly.

quotes.text: remember the more times you open the door, the quicker things will go off.

lines.text: Throw out bad or rotting food quickly, before it spoils other food.

quotes.text: throw out bad or rotting food before it spoils other food.
Throw out rotten or contaminated food quickly so it doesn't spoil other food in the fridge.

lines.text: Keep food cold, clean and check the label.

quotes.text: Keep food cold, clean and check the label.

lines.text: FSANZ (Australia and New Zealand) suggests getting eskies with ice bricks or gel packs ready before a power cut. No New Zealand source mentions chilly bins or ice.

quotes.text: Prepare eskies with ice bricks or gel packs to keep food cold if the power goes out.

steps.title: Food in the fridge

lines.text: The sources only give times for a fridge whose door was kept shut. None says how to tell how warm the food got, or what to do if the door was opened a lot. None mentions using a thermometer.

quotes.text: Unopened fridges should hold refrigeration temperature for 4 hours.

ask.question: How long has the fridge been without power?

steps.title: Fridge food should still be cold

lines.text: All the sources say an unopened fridge is still cold at this point.

quotes.text: An unopened refrigerator will keep your food cool for at least 2 hours.
Unopened fridges should hold refrigeration temperature for 4 hours.

lines.text: Keep the door shut. Eat fridge food first, starting with foods that will expire soon, such as bread, meat, salads and dairy products.

quotes.text: Eat foods that will expire soon first – such as bread, meat, salads, and dairy products.
Eat the food in your fridge first, then your freezer

steps.title: Fridge food: 2 to 4 hours

lines.text: MPI, NEMA, the QLDC poster and FSANZ say an unopened fridge holds its cold for about 4 hours.

quotes.text: Unopened fridges should hold refrigeration temperature for 4 hours.
A fridge should keep food cold for around four hours - after that it can begin to spoil.

lines.text: Northland Regional Council says "at least 2 hours". That is a minimum, not a limit, so it does not say the food is warm after 2 hours.

quotes.text: An unopened refrigerator will keep your food cool for at least 2 hours.

lines.text: Northland: food at 5 degrees Celsius or above for more than 2 hours is much more likely to grow germs that cause illness.

quotes.text: Once food reaches the temperature of 5 degrees Celsius or above for more than 2 hours it greatly increases the risk of growth by microorganisms that can cause illness.

lines.text: Check each food. Does it smell or look different? Has the colour changed, or is it slimy? If so, bin it.

quotes.text: Does the food from your fridge, freezer or pantry smell or look different? Has the colour changed and does it have a slimy texture? If so, it's likely unsafe and should be binned.

lines.text: Don't taste food to see if it's OK. If in doubt, throw it out.

quotes.text: Don't taste it to see if it's OK.
If in doubt, throw it out.

steps.title: Fridge food may have warmed up

lines.text: If you're not sure how long it has been, treat the food as warmed up.

quotes.text: If in doubt, throw it out.

lines.text: Northland: don't use fridge food that has warmed up. The only exceptions are butter or margarine, hard cheeses, raw eggs still in their shells, fruit and vegetables.

quotes.text: Do not use frozen food that has thawed or refrigerated food that has warmed up. The only exceptions to this are butter/margarine, hard cheeses, raw eggs (still in eggshells), fruit and vegetables.

lines.text: Auckland Regional Public Health Service (in a news item during a long power cut): "after today", meat and fish from the fridge may not be safe. It gives no number of hours. Raw vegetables, cheese and bread can still be eaten (it says "cheese", not only hard cheese).

quotes.text: After today, highly perishable foods in the fridge like meat and fish may not be safe to eat,
You can still eat food like raw vegetables, cheese and bread.

lines.text: Check every food you keep. Does it smell or look different? Has the colour changed, or is it slimy? If so, bin it.

quotes.text: Does the food from your fridge, freezer or pantry smell or look different? Has the colour changed and does it have a slimy texture? If so, it's likely unsafe and should be binned.

lines.text: Don't taste food to see if it's OK. If in doubt, throw it out.

quotes.text: Don't taste it to see if it's OK.
IF IN DOUBT, THROW IT OUT!

lines.text: No source covers leftovers, cooked rice, sliced meats, sauces, baby formula, breast milk, or medicines kept in the fridge (such as insulin). For health advice, ARPHS says call Healthline free on 0800 611 116.

quotes.text: For health advice call Healthline for free anytime on 0800 611 116

steps.title: Food in the freezer

lines.text: Check the frozen food now the power is back on. Look at one food at a time.

steps.title: Still frozen: you can refreeze it

lines.text: MPI: if the food still has ice crystals and the packaging isn't damaged or open, you can safely refreeze it.

quotes.text: If the food is still visibly frozen (for example, if it still has ice crystals on it) and the packaging isn't damaged or open, you can safely refreeze it.
If the frozen food has ice crystals and the packaging is intact then it can be refrozen.

lines.text: If the packaging is damaged or open, no source says it is safe to refreeze. If in doubt, throw it out.

steps.title: Tins and pantry food

lines.text: Eat your canned and non-perishable pantry foods last.

quotes.text: Eat your canned and non-perishable pantry foods last.

lines.text: Throw out any cans that are dented, swollen, damaged or leaking. (MPI: don't use tins that have broken open, are deeply dented or heavily rusted.)

quotes.text: Check canned foods and throw out any cans that are dented, swollen, damaged or leaking.
Do not use any tinned food that has been damaged (for example, if the can has broken open, become deeply dented, or is heavily rusted).

lines.text: If there was flooding: throw away all food (except cans) and drinking water that touched floodwater, including twist-top bottles and food in containers.

quotes.text: Throw away all food (except cans) and drinking water that have come into contact with floodwater, including items in twist-top bottles or stored in containers.

lines.text: If there was a fire: FSANZ says throw out food that has been near the fire, including food in cans and jars, even if it looks OK.

quotes.text: Throw out food that has been near fire, including food in cans and jars even if they appear OK.

steps.title: Cooking and clean hands

lines.text: Always wash and dry your hands before preparing food. If water is short, keep some in a bowl with disinfectant.

quotes.text: Always wash and dry your hands before preparing food - if water is in short supply keep some in a bowl with disinfectant.

lines.text: Make sure all utensils are clean before use.

quotes.text: ensure all utensils are clean before use

lines.text: Cook food thoroughly.

quotes.text: Cook food thoroughly.

lines.text: Throw out cooked food if it can't be kept in a fridge or eaten straight away.

quotes.text: Throw out cooked food if it can not be refrigerated or eaten immediately.

lines.text: Put food waste in bin bags, so it doesn't attract rats, mice and flies.

quotes.text: Place food waste in bin bags to avoid attracting rats, mice, and flies.
